font:SdfOldRegular>FRANKFORT - Governor Cal Fairweather has reassured Brandenburg's mayor that the long-promised federal funds for the rebuild- ing of Brandenburg are "on the way."                Despite an overwhelming early response following the tornado on April 18, which saw ample aid provided for residents in the aftermath, promised federal funds for re- building have still not arrived, with buildings patched up with wood, and major damage still evident.                                                      Early warnings meant many residents were taking shelter when the tornado touched down in the northeast part of town, but the high winds killed three residents and injured dozens. The F2 tornado destroyed cars and razed houses. Hundreds of people remain homeless, living in hotels or trailer parks paid for by the state, with others living with relatives or friends. Up to 40%% of residences and 30%% of businesses in the area are uninsured, meaning the cost to the taxpayer could exceed 50 million dollars. We wish to thank all our readers for being with us through these unprecedented times. If you are one of the few immune, you are the steward of a new world. It's now your duty to carry on the light of humanity and civilization. Even a single candle will cut through the deepest darkness. Avoid crowds at all costs.                                 As we saw at the boundary, gunfire attracts them. Have a baseball bat or other easy-to-use weapon ready and don't be afraid to attack them. the military's total refusal to answer questions about what is going on, carries eerie echoes of recent stand-offs between federal authorities and various armed groups.                          While  those  groups in general were almost certainly hostile and very dangerous, the new oper- ation  will  add  fuel to the fires of conspiracy theo- rists, including American separatist movements and anti-federalists, who see the federal government as increasingly trampling on the rights of its citizens. Hundreds of military personnel, fully armed and in battle gear, arrived in the area early Tuesday morning, encircling thou- sands of civilians within the cordon, as well as displacing hundreds of people who live outside the boundary. Rumors abound of a military exercise, but all calls to army officials went unanswered.                      Telephone lines have also been down in the area for the last several days, making communication with the cordoned-off area almost impossible.                     One West Point resi- dent, Larry Stoddard, said that after finishing his usual night shift as a nurse in Louisville, he saw, "soldiers  in  the  distance.<type:text, x:180, y:716, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular>Not unusual in Knox, but then I saw them putting up a fence all along the road. And yet, despite attempts by many residents to look on the bright side and downplay the threat, it's clear many feel a gnawing anxiety about the Knox Virus.              Authorities are now saying that the virus, though deadly, spreads only through fluid contact, drawing comparisons to ebola outbreaks, which were eventually contained. But  there's  never  been an ebola outbreak so near to a major city, and some residents have already relocated over the Ohio River. Others are making plans  to  join  them,  and<type:texture, width:146, height:1, x:680, y:786, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9><type:text, x:826, y:798, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, pivotX:1, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular>(See "Silence", A13)<type:text, x:15, y:195, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldBold>By Molly Aoide<type:text, x:15, y:211, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular>Staff Writer<type:text, x:15, y:240, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.4, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular>    GENEVA, Switzerland - Millions of travelers were thrown into limbo when the World Health Organi- zation on Sunday advised that all flights, excluding military and medical ones, be  suspended  worldwide to stop the "Knox Virus" spreading.                                 Though the WHO lacks any legal authority to  enforce  the  advice, all flights were grounded almost immediately by airlines shocked at the sudden nature of the an- nouncement.                             In a White House briefing,  the  President has called the WHO's an- nouncement "unwelcome and economically un- sound".                                    Air Erin CEO Ryan Byrne  said,  "We  knew this was coming, but we thought  we'd  at  least have time to prepare. We have to  comply.  None  of us want to be responsible for an outbreak, but we have businesses to run. The  cure  can't  be worse than the disease.<type:text, x:180, y:716, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular> The earthquake, estimated at 7.5 on the Richter scale, created a tsunami which inundated parts of the island of Hokkaido and struck coast of southeastern Russia.             Hundreds of people are feared dead, with fires and a landslide reported in the town of Okushiri on the small island of the same name near Hokkaido. The city was previously struck by a strong earthquake last January, which killed two people and injured more than a thousand. Monday's quake was far more devastating,     with     the<type:texture, width:146, height:1, x:680, y:786, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9><type:text, x:826, y:798, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, pivotX:1, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular>(See "Japan", A13)<type:text, x:15, y:195, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldBold>By Richard Carlson<type:text, x:15, y:211, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular>Staff Writer<type:text, x:15, y:240, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:380, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular>     KNOX EXCLUSION ZONE  BORDER,  Ky.  - A new photograph that emerged Monday of an in- fected, dismembered, but apparently still-living man in a street full of bodies in the town of West Point within the Knox Exclusion Zone has raised more questions about the government's response to the Knox Event.                        Thousands of resi- dents have been trapped within a cordoned-off zone of hundreds of square miles of Kentucky since July 6, with little commu- nication with the outside world. Heavy live fire failed to stop the large group's advance.                      Up to 100 Army per- sonnel and civilians were killed, with many hun- dreds wounded. Witnesses report the sounds of battle attracted even more of the infected from a wide area. Both military and refugees near the border pulled back to Louisville.                    Large groups of the infected  attacked  houses in the suburbs throughout the day, moving slowly north towards the city, meeting only sporadic re- sistance, mostly by armed civilians. The streets and bridges out of Louisville quickly filled with panick- ed citizens fleeing over the Ohio River, and traffic jams have  been  reported<type:text, x:180, y:716, r:0, g:0, b:0, a:0.9, scaleX:0.4, scaleY:0.4, autoWidth:375, textTracking:0.5, textLeading:3, font:SdfOldRegular>as far north as Columbus, Ohio, and Indianapolis, Ind. Coalfield

Coalfield, Kentucky

A Taste of the Wild West

Founded in the 1850s as a stop for travelers heading east, Coalfield became notorious for a series of conflicts between Sheriff Everett Holloway and Irvin Bradshaw and his gang.
The feud culminated with a massive shootout on the night of August 11, 1882, which ended when the Lawman's Distillery caught fire and exploded, taking many buildings with it. No sign of Everett Holloway or Irvin Bradshaw was ever found.

Now you can visit the original site of Coalfield, renovated accurately. Visit our general store, have a drink in the saloons, experience life as a blacksmith, tour period cabins, and see what the Old West was really like!

Come along every Saturday for a reenactment of the shootout between Holloway's lawmen and the Bradshaw gang!

March Ridge Cold War Bunker

Tour a Future that didn't happen!

Just off Adams Road in northern March Ridge sits a fenced area with a small shed and a radio tower.

For decades, this was the entrance to a top secret nuclear bunker, built to house Fort Knox's military leaders.

Built four storeys underground in 1960, with thick steel doors, the bunker was made to withstand a direct nuclear hit on Fort Knox itself.

Space was limited, with beds for only forty people. It's unlikely the bunker would have survived for long without resupply.

Thankfully, armageddon did not arrive.

The bunker was decommissioned in 1991 and is now available for weekend tours!

Book ahead on 943-555-7843.

Note: Tour not suitable for the claustrophobic or young children. Bunker has not been fully checked for asbestos and some forms of poisoning. Waivers must be signed on entry.

Creating a Faction

Click on %1, then Create Faction to create an invite-only group, with private chat. <LINE> PvP can be disabled against fellow members, and members show on each other's Maps. <LINE> Note: faction members don't necessarily share Safehouses, which is done using the Safehouse menu.
Using the Chatbox

Press %1 to type in chat. Your chat can be preceded by commands: /all (global chat, won't attract zombies), /say or /s (local chat), /whisper or /w followed by username (private message), <LINE> /yell or /y (shout), /safehouse or /sh (safehouse members), /faction or /f (faction members), <LINE> /admin or /a (admin chat), /r or /radio (message using equipped radio).

Medical Checking
Use %1 on a player and select the option to perform a Medical Check. <LINE> Here you can provide aid to other players - or check for a dreaded bite mark.
